title: Acids, Bases and Salts — Chapter Summary
intro: Curd is sour; soap is bitter and slippery. The kitchen is full of acids and bases. In chemistry, an acid releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water and a base releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻). Their reactions and pH governs everything from why our stomach digests food, to why bee stings hurt, to why farmers add lime to acidic soil. This chapter explains the chemistry of acids, bases and salts, and uses the pH scale to put numbers on 'how acidic'.

sections.heading: Acids and Bases — Indicators
bullets: Acid: sour taste; turns blue litmus red; releases H⁺ in water.
Base: bitter taste, soapy feel; turns red litmus blue; releases OH⁻ in water.
Litmus: red in acid, blue in base. Methyl orange: red / yellow.
Phenolphthalein: colourless / pink.
Universal indicator: red (strong acid) → green (neutral) → purple (strong base).

sections.heading: Reactions of Acids
bullets: Acid + Metal → Salt + H₂↑. (Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑.)
Acid + Metal carbonate → Salt + H₂O + CO₂↑. (Limestone fizzes in vinegar.)
Acid + Metallic oxide → Salt + H₂O. (Neutralisation.)
CO₂ test: turns lime water milky.

sections.heading: Reactions of Bases
bullets: Base + Non-metallic oxide → Salt + H₂O. (2 NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.)
Base + Acid → Salt + H₂O. (Neutralisation.)
Some bases react with metals: Zn + 2 NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂↑.

sections.heading: What Acids and Bases Have in Common
bullets: All acids release H⁺ ions in water (forms H₃O⁺).
All alkaline bases release OH⁻ ions.
Strong vs weak: STRONG acid/base ionises COMPLETELY in water; WEAK ionises PARTIALLY.
Concentrated vs dilute: about AMOUNT per litre — independent of strength.
Always pour ACID INTO WATER (never water into acid) — dilution is highly exothermic and adding water to acid can splash dangerously.

sections.heading: The pH Scale
bullets: Scale 0 to 14. 7 = neutral. < 7 acidic; > 7 basic.
Each unit = 10× change in [H⁺]. pH 3 has 10× more H⁺ than pH 4.
pH of common substances: lemon ≈ 2, vinegar ≈ 3, water = 7, blood = 7.4, soap ≈ 10, drain cleaner ≈ 14.
Tooth decay: enamel dissolves below pH 5.5.
Acid rain: pH < 5.5 from dissolved SO₂, NO₂.
Soil pH: most plants prefer pH 6-7.5; lime (basic) cures acidic soil.
Bee sting (acidic) — relieve with baking soda. Wasp sting (alkaline) — relieve with vinegar.

sections.heading: Salts and Their Industries
bullets: Salt = product of acid + base. pH depends on parent acid/base strengths.
Common salt (NaCl) is the raw material for many industrial chemicals.
Chlor-alkali: 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → 2 NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂. Gives soap, PVC, fuel.
Bleaching powder: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂. Bleaches fabric, disinfects water.
Baking soda (NaHCO₃) — in baking, antacid, fire extinguishers.
Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10 H₂O) — detergents, glass-making.
Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½ H₂O) — hardens with water; used for casts.
Water of crystallisation: CuSO₄·5 H₂O blue → CuSO₄ white on heating.

key_takeaways: Acid + Metal → Salt + H₂; Acid + Carbonate → Salt + H₂O + CO₂; Acid + Metal oxide → Salt + H₂O.
Base + Non-metallic oxide → Salt + H₂O; Acid + Base → Salt + H₂O (neutralisation).
All acids share H⁺; all bases share OH⁻ when dissolved in water.
Strong vs weak (ionisation); concentrated vs dilute (amount).
Always pour acid into water — never the reverse.
Practical pH: tooth decay below 5.5; acid rain below 5.5; antacids neutralise excess stomach acid.
Salts from common salt: NaOH, Cl₂, H₂, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda; plaster of Paris from gypsum.

glossary.definition: A substance that releases H⁺ ions in water and turns blue litmus red.
A substance that releases OH⁻ ions in water (alkaline) and turns red litmus blue.
The product of the reaction between an acid and a base.
A substance that changes colour to show whether a solution is acidic or basic.
Reaction between an acid and a base producing salt and water.
An acid or base that ionises COMPLETELY in water (e.g. HCl, NaOH).
An acid or base that ionises PARTIALLY in water (e.g. acetic acid, NH₃).
A solution with a large amount of solute per unit volume.
A solution with a small amount of solute per unit volume.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or basic a solution is; 7 is neutral.
Rain with a pH below 5.5 due to dissolved SO₂ and NO₂.
A mild base used to neutralise excess stomach acid (e.g. NaHCO₃, Mg(OH)₂).
Electrolysis of brine producing NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
CaSO₄·½ H₂O, made by heating gypsum; sets to gypsum when mixed with water.
Water molecules that are part of a crystal's structure (e.g. CuSO₄·5 H₂O).
